title: Comfort the afflicted
tomorrow: Peter asked for a number. what did he get back?

cards: Sympathy cards fill a whole aisle, and some of the lines inside try to explain: everything happens for a reason, she's in a better place. The book of Job starts somewhere else.
Three friends hear about Job's losses and come together to comfort him. From a distance they hardly know him. They weep and tear their garments.
Then they sit down with him on the ground, seven days and seven nights, and nobody speaks a word, because they see how great his grief is.

teach.h: THE SILENT DAYS WERE THE BEST.
teach.b: Here's why the silence was their best moment. When Job finally speaks, the friends start answering, and chapter after chapter they explain his suffering to him. The explanations wound.

At the end of the book, God tells them they have not spoken rightly, as his servant Job has. So the story holds both halves of comfort: what helps, and what doesn't. Jesus shows the first half at Bethany.
Lazarus has died, and his sister Mary falls at Jesus's feet weeping.
John's Gospel says simply, "And Jesus wept." He's about to call Lazarus out of the tomb, and still he doesn't hurry past the tears.
Paul puts it in one line to the Romans: "weep with them that weep."
Comforting the afflicted is on the traditional list of spiritual works of mercy, and it rarely needs the perfect sentence. A chair pulled up. A meal left on a porch.

A call that's mostly quiet. Look back over the week and it's the same move every day: the visit, the letter, the grave, the walk, the seat beside the learner, the private word. Mercy keeps showing up in person.

how: Catholics bring meals and keep company with grieving families, some parishes have bereavement ministries, and the Church keeps praying for the dead and the mourning at funerals and anniversary Masses.

o: stay with someone who is hurting
cheer up a person who is sad

p: seven silent days on the ground
God says they did not speak rightly

s: Job's friends helped him most with their explanations
their best days were the silent ones. at the end, God says they did not speak rightly.
Jesus wept for Lazarus even though he was about to raise him
John says Jesus wept. he didn't hurry past the grief.
comforting someone means finding the words that fix it
it rarely needs the perfect sentence: a chair, a meal, a quiet call.

games.q: your friend's dog died this morning. she texts you a photo of its empty bed. what's the comfort move?
o: go over or call, and mostly just be there with her.
remind her he had a long, good life, so it's okay.
send a link on the stages of grief to help her process.
games.why: Job's friends helped most while they sat in silence, and Jesus wept with Mary before anything else. explanations can wait.

practice: Close your eyes and bring to mind someone who is hurting right now. Don't plan what to say to them.
Just sit beside them in your mind, the way Job's friends sat on the ground, and let the quiet be the gift; if you pray, you can hold them before God without any words at all.

wordCard.voice: Comfort the afflicted. Stay with someone in their pain, and let presence do most of the talking.

orig.note: Greek: he wept. John 11:35, Jesus with Lazarus's sister Mary.

carryVoice: Your line: sit with them. Job's friends did it best before they said a single word. A week of mercy, kept.
